summary: Describes how 3270 display terminal data is transferred using existing Telnet capabilities, the practice traditionally called TN3270.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1576 explains how IBM 3270 terminal data was carried over Telnet. A client and a server agree on a few Telnet options first, then swap whole screens of mainframe data instead of characters.

questions: how does tn3270 work over telnet
which telnet options does tn3270 use
what are the 3270 attn and sysreq keys
how are 3270 screens separated on the wire
subtitle: How IBM 3270 mainframe terminal data was carried over ordinary Telnet connections, as practiced by vendors.

tldr.problem: IBM 3270 display terminals use block mode data in EBCDIC, which differs from ordinary Telnet, yet people on IP networks needed to reach existing IBM mainframes.
tldr.mechanism: TN3270 negotiates three existing Telnet options, Terminal-Type, Binary Transmission and End of Record, and then exchanges 3270 data streams, each one ended with IAC EOR. The SNA keys ATTN and SYSREQ are mapped onto existing Telnet commands.
tldr.outcome: The memo records what vendors already did and defines no new Telnet option or command. RFC 1041 had tried to standardise this with a 3270 Regime option, but very few developers and vendors ever implemented it.

today: RFC 1576 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes practice as of January 1994 and notes that very few developers and vendors ever implemented the 3270 Regime option of RFC 1041.

sections.title: Why TN3270 Differs from Plain Telnet
sections.content:
3270 display terminal data differs from traditional terminal data in two ways. It is block mode, so a whole screen arrives at once, and it uses EBCDIC instead of ASCII for characters. The memo says these two differences are the primary reason for separating TN3270 from standard Telnet.

The motivation is in section 2. Existing complex IBM 3270 display terminal networks are not easily integrated with the growing number of multi-platform networking environments, specifically TCP/IP. To make it easy to connect display terminals to 3270 hosts over IP networks, several vendors introduced Telnet servers that give TCP/IP users a connection to existing IBM mainframes by supporting display terminal emulation using a subset of the existing Telnet protocol. Such a server may sit on the host itself, or be connected to the host using SNA or non-SNA methods. IBM terminals are generically called 3270s, which includes a broad range of terminals and devices, not all of which actually begin with the numbers 327x.

In an SNA network a 3270 terminal has two sessions with the host: one for the host application and one for the SSCP, the System Services Control Point that links the terminal to the host computer. For TN3270 this distinction does not apply, because there is only a single Telnet session with the host or server. The SNA key that toggles between the two sessions is SYSREQ. A session in an SNA environment is identified by a Logical Unit name; in a non-SNA environment there is no LU name, and the closest thing to one in TN3270 is the client's IP address. TN3270 does not support typical SNA responses and is classified as a non-SNA protocol, and a TN3270 emulator is neither aware nor concerned about how the Telnet server reaches the 3270 host application.

Support for 3270 terminal emulation over Telnet is currently accomplished by what the memo calls the de facto standard of negotiating three separate Telnet options: Terminal-Type, Binary Transmission and End of Record. TN3270 makes use of existing Telnet options and defines no additional options or commands. RFC 1041 attempted to standardise the method by defining a 3270 Regime Telnet Option, but historically very few developers and vendors ever implemented it.
sections.plainLanguage: The old screens send a whole form at once, in a different alphabet from most computers. Those two differences are why this needed its own treatment instead of plain Telnet.

sections.title: Connection Negotiation
sections.content:
Clients connect to TCP port 23, the Telnet port. The order in which the terminal type, EOR and BINARY options are negotiated is not significant. The memo gives a typical connection: the server asks for TERMINAL-TYPE and the client agrees, the server asks for the terminal type and the client answers with a string such as IBM-3278-2. The terminal type string gives the terminal model, the type and its support of enhanced attribute bytes, and the acceptable values are listed in RFC 1340, although other values are in use that do not appear there.

The model suffix selects the screen size, because 3270 terminals can switch between the standard 24x80 screen and an alternate size. Model -2 is 24x80, the same as the standard size, model -3 is 32x80, model -4 is 43x80 and model -5 is 27x132. Appending the two character string -E to the terminal type means the terminal can handle the 3270 extended data stream, that is, structured fields. Some server implementations read -E as meaning the terminal can handle extended attributes such as highlighting, field validation, character set and outlining. The 3279 series of terminals is capable of extended attributes while the 3278 series is not.

After that the server offers EOR and BINARY, the client answers, and the two sides exchange 3270 data streams terminated with IAC EOR. To end the connection, one of the session partners closes the socket, typically the server when the user logs off of the host. A server that wants to return to NVT mode may send IAC WONT BINARY or IAC WONT EOR, and either one of those causes the connection to no longer satisfy the requirements for a valid TN3270 session, so the client then processes data from the server as NVT ASCII data.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers agree on a few ground rules first, such as what kind of screen it is and how to mark where one message ends. After that they swap whole screens.

sections.title: Sending 3270 Data
sections.content:
The 3270 data stream consists of a command and its associated data. Commands include, but are not limited to, erase screen, erase and write to screen, and read current screen.

The reason for negotiating the EOR Telnet option is to provide a way of separating these commands, since no length information is specified. The memo is precise about the rule: 3270 commands are interpreted by the Telnet client in their entirety, and each 3270 command and its possible data is terminated with the IAC EOR sequence.

The Binary option is also required, because 3270 data may contain the FF hexadecimal byte, which is the IAC character. When that byte appears during a TN3270 connection it is handled as the Binary option requires. The memo also covers how a server checks that the client is still there. The NOP command, hexadecimal F1, is used by some servers to test for the continued presence of a client, and the client does not respond to it; if a client has terminated abnormally, TCP/IP send errors occur. The Timing Mark option serves the same purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Each screen is sent as one parcel with a special stamp at the end, so the receiver knows where it stops even though the data carries no length.

sections.title: 3270 Structured Fields
sections.content:
3270 structured fields give a much wider range of features than old-style 3270 data, such as support for graphics, partitions and IPDS printer data streams. A structured field is a 3270 data type that lets data which is not itself 3270 data be embedded within 3270 data. A structured field consists of the structured field command followed by one or more data blocks, and each data block has a length and a structured field identifier, followed optionally by additional data.

Not every TN3270 client can be expected to support all structured field functions, so there must be a mechanism for clients that support some or all of them to say so. The memo says this is typically done by adding -E to the end of the terminal type string: when the terminal identifies itself as able to handle extended attributes, it is also able to send and receive structured fields. The design of structured fields also provides a convenient way to convey the level of support, including no support, for the various functions. That mechanism is the Read Partition Query command, which the host application sends to the client. The client answers with a Query Reply listing which, if any, structured field functions it supports. A client that does not support structured fields can still identify at least this structured field and reply with a null set, and the memo leaves the exact sequence of events to the client implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some screens carry extra data such as graphics or printer output. The client tells the host which of these extras it can handle, and the host asks before sending them.

sections.title: The ATTN and SYSREQ Keys
sections.content:
The 3270 ATTN key is interpreted by many host applications in an SNA environment as a sign that the user wants to interrupt the execution of the current process. A majority of the Telnet servers currently accept the Telnet IAC BREAK command, code 243, to signal this event. Using the key takes two things. The client maps a single key or a combination of keys to the 3270 ATTN key, and transmits a Telnet BREAK command to the server when the user presses it. The server translates the BREAK command into the right form and passes it to the host application as an ATTN key; in other words, a server representing an SLU in an SNA session sends a SIGNAL RU to the host application. The ATTN key is not supported in a non-SNA environment, so a TN3270 server representing non-SNA 3270 devices ignores any Telnet BREAK commands it receives.

The 3270 SYSREQ key is useful where the Telnet server is attached to the host using SNA, in particular when the host application becomes locked or the user wants to end the session without closing the Telnet connection. Some Telnet servers interpret the Telnet Interrupt Process command as a SYSREQ key, and others recognise the 3270 Test Request key as a SYSREQ key. In an SNA environment, pressing the key toggles the terminal between the host application session and the SSCP session; the user usually enters LOGOFF once it has been pressed to end the application session and then selects a new host, and sometimes pressing SYSREQ again unlocks the host application so that normal activity resumes.

It is up to the Telnet server to interpret the command and send the right commands to the host, and to format the resulting host data for display on the client. The data format during the SSCP session differs slightly from normal 3270 data, and since the server has no way to pass that data straight to the client, it must either handle it itself and ignore SYSREQ events or convert it to 3270 data for display. To implement SYSREQ, clients provide a key or combination of keys mapped to the 3270 SYSREQ key and transmit a Telnet IP command or a Test Request key, depending on the server. Servers representing non-SNA 3270 terminals may ignore such commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Two special buttons on the old keyboard are turned into Telnet signals. The server then turns them back into button presses for the mainframe.

sections.title: What TN3270 Does Not Cover
sections.content:
The memo lists what current TN3270 implementations do not support. There is no capability for clients to emulate the 328x class of printers. There is no mechanism by which a Telnet client can request that a connection be associated with a given 3270 device name, which matters when a terminal session is established because many host applications behave differently depending on the network name of the terminal. The ATTN and SYSREQ keys are not universally supported.

There is no support for the SNA positive and negative response process. All data that is sent is assumed to have been either handled or ignored. The memo explains that a negative response indicates some sort of error at the client while processing the previously received data, for example the host application building a data stream with an invalid command or a mechanical error at the client, while positive responses indicate that processing of the previously received data has completed. The lack of SNA response processing is part of what makes TN3270 efficient. There is also no mechanism by which the client can access the SNA BIND information, which describes in detail the session between the Telnet server and the host application. Finally, the connection negotiation does not make it clear whether clients should support 3270 structured fields.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence long: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The list admits some things this setup cannot do, such as pretending to be a printer or telling the host exactly which screen it is.

viz.caption: THE THREE TELNET OPTIONS TN3270 NEGOTIATES

items.label: BINARY
items.desc: Lets 3270 data carry the FF byte, which is the Telnet IAC character.

items.label: TERMINAL-TYPE
items.desc: Carries the terminal model and screen size, for example IBM-3278-2.

items.label: EOR
items.desc: Ends each 3270 command and its data with IAC EOR.

messages.label: IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE SEND IAC SE
IAC SB TERMINAL-TYPE IS IBM-3278-2 IAC SE
IAC DO EOR, IAC WILL EOR
messages.note: The client answers IAC WILL EOR, IAC DO EOR.

messages.label: IAC DO BINARY, IAC WILL BINARY
messages.note: The client answers IAC WILL BINARY, IAC DO BINARY.

messages.label: 3270 data stream, IAC EOR
messages.note: The client replies in the same form.

viz.caption: OTHER TELNET OPTIONS AND COMMANDS A TN3270 SESSION MAY SEE

items.title: 3270-REGIME
items.text: Offered by few servers. A client that does not support it answers WONT.

items.title: SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD
items.text: Requested by some servers. TN3270 never sends the go ahead character.

items.title: ECHO
items.text: Used when a server asks for a user name or password before the session starts.

items.title: TIMING-MARK
items.text: Used by some servers to test whether the client is still present.

items.title: NOP
items.text: Another presence test. The client ignores it and does not answer.

items.title: BREAK, code 243
items.text: Sent by the client for the 3270 ATTN key.

items.title: Interrupt Process
items.text: Sent by the client for the 3270 SYSREQ key, on some servers.
